rv.q: The same goes for every aspect of this terrific play in what must surely be its ideal production.
Smartly directed by Daniel Sullivan, the often-caustic production provides a humane, realistic and absorbing examination of ordinary people's behavior when their world is threatened.
Ms. Lindsay-Abaire has written a solidly crafted play that asks hard questions about class, loyalty and the meaning of success in contemporary America.
In the current economy of scaled-back American dreams, when the role of class is too often dismissed, Good People has a quality rarely seen on Broadway: It seems necessary.

And McDormand captures all of Margaret's contradictions with sensitivity and depth, and the haggard, haunted look of a hamster that's spent too long on the treadmill but lacks the wherewithal and the means to stop.

Rabbit Hole, which he adapted for a 2010 film, focused on an attractive, accomplished couple whose seemingly charmed life was shattered by the accidental death of their 4-year-old son. In contrast, the central figure in Lindsay-Abaire's excellent new play, Good People (* * * ½ out of four), is a woman for whom things can only get better.
Director Daniel Sullivan can’t finesse the play’s contrivances.
Renée Elise Goldsberry is best when scrambling to avoid the inadvertent cultural condescension this highly educated daughter of an African-American doctor keeps stumbling into with Margaret.
McDormand’s performance raises the stakes on Abaire’s drama, sparking moments of suspense amidst basically banal material.
It remains fixed, insisting we come to meet it despite its not providing us a single compelling argument to do so.
Good People” is a new play by David Lindsay-Abaire, whose works range from screwy comedies like “Kimberly Akimbo” to the heartbreaking Pulitzer-winner “Rabbit Hole.

aw.sub: Won Best Actress in a Play

cn.t: Lindsay-Abaire's class-conscious drama draws mostly positive reviews for its authentic portrayal of working-class Boston and McDormand's forceful lead performance, though some critics find the play itself underwhelming.

vs.sum: The Samuel J. Friedman Theatre offers good sightlines with minimal obstructions and a well-raked mezzanine, ensuring a clear view from most seats. The sound quality is consistently praised, and the seating is comfortable with decent legroom. The theater's ambiance is enhanced by its elegant design following renovation, though facilities like restrooms are average, leading to some congestion during intermissions.

acc.note: Elevator to all levels. Built-in induction loop for t-coil hearing aids.
